lms_catalog.short_description: Read OCP cluster designs, compare AI fabric choices and assemble the evidence for deployment.
lms_catalog.overview: This four-module course applies OCP Open Cluster Designs for AI contributions to practical design review. Learners trace pod groups into complete clusters, compare training and inference fabric choices, and connect the selected configuration to physical, validation and operating evidence.
lms_catalog.duration_note: Includes narration, diagram reading, activities and eight questions. Optional external recordings and reference reading are outside the estimate.

slides.transcript: Welcome to Open Cluster Designs for AI. This course turns the system view from Open Systems for AI into a practical way to read a cluster design. You will follow a building block into a complete cluster, compare training and inference fabric choices, and decide what evidence is needed before deployment.

slides.title: From a Published Design to a Defensible Decision
slides.transcript: The course has four modules and an estimated learner time of fifty-five minutes. First, locate the architecture and its assumptions. Next, trace equipment and connections from a pod group into a cluster. Then compare fabric choices against the workload. Finally, assemble the evidence for an installation and operating handoff. slides.title: Start with the Workload and the Design Boundary
slides.transcript: Start with a workload description, not a shopping list. A training service, an independent model-serving service, and a model distributed across several hosts can place very different demands on the same accelerator count. Record the form factor, the communication pattern, the storage demands, the tenant boundaries, and the performance goals. Include the operating team and the facility in that conversation. A published design becomes useful when those assumptions are visible. A different assumption does not make the reference useless. It tells you which part of the design needs another check. The Open Cluster Designs initiative develops practical building blocks and complete cluster architectures to reduce repeated integration work. It works alongside Open Data Centers for AI within the wider Open Systems for AI effort. The preceding course provides that broader system context.

slides.title: From Compute Domains to Complete Clusters
slides.transcript: Read the hierarchy from the compute domain outward. An xPU is a generic accelerator. In the January example, an xPU-node is a server containing eight accelerators and the resources they need. Its high-bandwidth scale-up connections are inside that server. A larger scale-up pod can have a different physical shape, including a rack-scale arrangement. An Open Pod Group, or OPG-M, combines compute domains with networking, storage, management, and supporting infrastructure. M denotes the accelerator count in that group. An XOC-N is a complete scale-out cluster containing N accelerators. It combines one or more pod groups with the shared resources needed at cluster level. Follow those boundaries in the animation. A node is not a pod group, and a pod group is not automatically a complete cluster. These are architectural domains. Their physical packaging can change.

slides.title: Give Each Network a Clear Job
slides.transcript: A cluster contains several kinds of traffic. Scale-up communication stays within a high-bandwidth compute domain. Scale-out communication connects those domains. The January architecture also separates a CPU-facing scale-out network, called SO-C, from storage. An in-band network supports host management and services. A separate out-of-band network reaches hardware management controllers and supports recovery when the host operating system is unavailable. The April references use SO-C and front-end terminology for the CPU-facing service path and offer configurations that converge it with storage. Read the function and the chosen configuration together. Six named functions do not always require six separately built physical fabrics. Equally, combining traffic does not remove its capacity, policy, or failure requirements. Connections between clusters or across distance introduce another boundary; they are not a complete design supplied by these single-cluster examples.

slides.title: Choose the Document That Answers the Question
slides.transcript: Use the document set as a map. The Open Cluster Designs white paper explains the purpose, hierarchy, and design objectives. The January OPG-M architecture describes the pod-group hardware example. Its companion XOC-N architecture adds the shared networks and head-end resources for a complete cluster. The April training and inference fabric references provide network-centric implementation guidance, including topology, declarative management, traffic policy, and operating workflows. They use Hedgehog and SONiC as a contributed implementation. That does not make those products a requirement for every open cluster. Record the document, revision, form factor, and configuration you are using. A published hardware architecture, a particular fabric implementation, and a preview of future work answer different questions.

slides.title: Match a Proposal to a Published Baseline
slides.transcript: Consider a proposal for liquid-cooled rack-scale compute that cites the January air-cooled server design. Before accepting its equipment list, identify what changed. The compute domain may now span a rack. The number and placement of network interfaces may differ. So can power, cooling, cable reach, storage attachment, and the management inventory. The April fabric references do discuss both air and liquid cooling, but their stated compute unit is still an eight-accelerator server with scale-up inside the enclosure. A cooling-independent logical fabric is not a complete qualification of a different compute form factor. Pause and identify the assumptions you would put on the review list. Then keep the references that still apply and ask for evidence at the changed boundaries.

slides.title: Read the OPG-128 as a Complete Building Block
slides.transcript: The January OPG-128 example contains sixteen servers with eight accelerators each. Sixteen times eight gives one hundred twenty-eight accelerators. The published physical example uses nine racks, with compute, networking, storage, management, and supporting equipment distributed across the group. Its assumptions include air cooling and four-hundred-gigabit scale-out links. Those are properties of this example, not universal limits on an Open Pod Group. Notice what the accelerator count leaves out: the storage and metadata services, network switches, power support, cable management, and the paths used to operate and recover the equipment. The complete building block includes all those responsibilities. A new supplier choice or a different rack density still needs to satisfy the interfaces and site requirements.

slides.title: Reconcile the Kit with the Chosen Configuration
slides.transcript: Read the bill of materials alongside the rack layout and connection maps. The list tells you what to procure. The layout tells you where it goes. The map tells you how identified endpoints connect. A configuration identifier and source revision should join those records. If a quantity in a summary table disagrees with a detailed topology or map, stop treating the list as a ready-to-order kit. Reconcile the discrepancy for the chosen configuration. Use reconciled entries for the selected configuration, rather than combining quantities from different variants. The transferable skill is to compare records, resolve differences, and preserve the result. An apparently complete document is a starting point for that work.

slides.title: Follow One Connection from Device to Device
slides.transcript: Follow two connections without losing their identities. In the OPG connection map, scale-out leaf one, labeled SOL1, uses port one with an eight-hundred-gigabit breakout connection. Its two four-hundred-gigabit legs reach node one, network interfaces one and five. They share a switch port but remain distinct endpoint connections. The next highlighted path is an uplink. Leaf SOL1, port two, optical-module port one, connects to scale-out spine one, port one, optical-module port one. In the cluster map, the same leaf appears as O1S1: pod group one, scale-out switch one. That alias matters when you join the two documents. A port number, a breakout leg, and an optical-module port are different parts of an endpoint identity. Checking speed alone would not detect a swapped destination. Use the complete identity, the medium, the reach, and the selected map together.

slides.title: Read the Published Clos Cluster
slides.transcript: Read this original Clos plan from the shared spine layer down to the pod groups. Eight scale-out spine switches sit across the top of the network. Along the bottom are eight OPG-128 building blocks. Each group has two fifty-one-terabit-class leaves, giving sixteen leaves across the cluster. The blue lines represent four-hundred-gigabit optical connections between the leaf and spine layers. The lower callout expands one leaf's connections toward the accelerator nodes. The port legend above the network explains how the document identifies a switch port and an optical-module port separately. An eight-hundred-gigabit OSFP module can expose two four-hundred-gigabit connections, so those identities still matter. This is a complete January example with specified hardware and port allocations. It does not establish the switch count for every possible Clos network. Compare it with the alternative wiring plan on the next slide, carrying the source revision and selected configuration with both drawings.

slides.title: Compare the Rail Plan at Cluster Scale
slides.transcript: Figure seven shows the rail-optimized scale-out plan for the same January XOC-1k example. Rails group network interfaces with matching accelerator affinity across servers. Count the eight OPG-128 groups along the bottom. Each group now has four twenty-six-terabit-class leaves, giving thirty-two leaves at cluster level. Eight fifty-one-terabit-class spine switches still form the shared scale-out layer. The optical links shown run at four hundred gigabits per second. Eight times one hundred twenty-eight still gives one thousand twenty-four accelerators. The attachment and selected switch configuration have changed. The April training reference makes a different comparison: single-homed and rail-optimized wiring on the same switch platform and port budget. There, the wiring choice does not itself change switch count. Keep those comparison conditions separate from the January quantities. This drawing shows the scale-out fabric. The complete cluster also needs storage, CPU-facing networks, management, and head-end services. Reconcile the pod-group and cluster-layer kits into that full deployment. Adding another group can consume capacity in shared switches and services even when the new group is internally complete.

slides.title: Account for the Shared Head-End Functions
slides.transcript: The head end is more than a login server. It provides client access and supports functions such as scheduling, image and container repositories, observability, and supporting storage. Hardware recovery also needs a reachable management path. Their resource requirements depend on the selected applications and operating model. The January architecture provides numerical examples, while explicitly asking designers to verify them for the target workload. Treat availability requirements by function. Two instances in a drawing are not proof that their power, network paths, state, or recovery procedures are independent. Identify the service owner and ask how capacity, failover, and restoration will be demonstrated. That makes the head end part of the design review, rather than equipment added after the compute order.

slides.title: Review the Next Expansion Before Ordering
slides.transcript: Now consider an expansion beyond the selected cluster example. The new group has the expected accelerator count and passes its local checks. What else must be reviewed? First, compare the new leaf uplinks with available spine ports and bandwidth. Next, check storage, client access, scheduling, repositories, and management capacity. Then update the end-to-end maps, rack and cable routes, and physical support requirements. The January utilization tables show that different shared networks have different amounts of spare capacity. Do not assume they all grow at the same rate. For the activity, choose the first records you would request before approving the expansion. A defensible answer links each added demand to an identified shared resource and an owner for its verification.

slides.title: Read the Variant Assumptions First
slides.transcript: Start by reading the variant assumptions. Both April references target servers with eight accelerators, whose high-bandwidth scale-up connections are inside the server. Their scale-out Ethernet fabric connects those servers. Logical topology and management can be reused across air-cooled and liquid-cooled deployments within that form factor. Physical layout, optics, cable lengths, power, cooling, and recovery paths still need site-specific checks. Record the number of scale-out network interfaces, their port speeds, the switch platform and breakout arrangement, the plane count, and the front-end and storage configuration. A label such as eight-hundred-gigabit switch does not mean every server link is eight hundred gigabits. The selected port mode and connection determine the link rate. Those assumptions also set the conditions for a fair topology comparison.

slides.title: Choose Wiring from the Traffic Pattern
slides.transcript: Watch where the traffic goes. With single-homed Clos wiring, the scale-out interfaces of a server attach to the same leaf. Traffic between servers on that leaf can remain local. Rail-optimized wiring groups interfaces by accelerator affinity. Within a first-hop rail domain, matching-rail traffic can remain on its leaf, while traffic between rails on different leaves crosses the spine. Both arrangements can use a Clos fabric. Here, we hold the schematic hardware constant and change the attachment pattern. Neither pattern wins for every workload. The useful question is how much traffic can stay local under the expected communication pattern and placement. A scheduler that knows the first-hop domains can help preserve that locality. The animation shows paths, not measured performance. Real results also depend on the fabric, host configuration, congestion, and workload behavior.

slides.title: Count Ports and Planes Separately
slides.transcript: Count the ports and their rates before assigning a benefit to two planes. One four-hundred-gigabit port provides a nominal four hundred gigabits per second. Two two-hundred-gigabit ports provide the same aggregate nominal rate. Two four-hundred-gigabit ports provide eight hundred in aggregate. In a dual-plane design, each port attaches to a different fabric plane. That separation can support maintenance and failure isolation. It does not automatically double bandwidth. If one of two equal-rate planes is unavailable, half the nominal aggregate port capacity remains. Whether the application continues successfully depends on its networking support, the failure, the remaining capacity, and the operating procedure. Keep those as acceptance questions. Compare the actual port configuration, not the words single-plane and dual-plane by themselves.

slides.title: Choose Separation for the Training Workload
slides.transcript: The training reference offers two separation profiles. Minimal Training converges CPU-facing front-end and storage traffic. Full Training separates those functions. Both retain the scale-out back-end used for communication between compute domains, as well as management paths. These names belong to this training reference. Minimal Training does not mean that the scale-out network disappears. Distributed training communication can use remote direct memory access, or RDMA. RDMA over Converged Ethernet is commonly called RoCE. In the contributed implementation, switch policy combines traffic classification, congestion signaling, and priority flow control for the designated traffic class. The hosts and network interfaces must be configured consistently too. Profile selection should follow the workload, storage behavior, isolation needs, and operating team, rather than a preference for the fewest network labels.

slides.title: Add an Inference Back-End When the Workload Needs It
slides.transcript: Inference uses a different decision. If each model-serving request is handled within one server, with no cross-host dependency on its critical path, the Minimal Inference profile omits the scale-out back-end. It still needs the front-end and storage path, a gateway for external service traffic, in-band management, and an independent out-of-band path. Now let the model or a critical dependency span hosts. The Distributed Inference profile adds back-end connectivity for that communication. It retains the front-end and storage arrangement and the gateway role. Follow that addition in the animation: an accelerator back-end appears because the workload needs it. Do not confuse Minimal Inference with Minimal Training. Also, a service can have many independent serving hosts without requiring a back-end between them. The dependency pattern, rather than server count alone, drives this choice.

slides.title: Keep Gateway Capacity and Tenant Policy Explicit
slides.transcript: External service traffic makes the gateway and tenant boundaries important. In the contributed inference implementation, tenant networks use separate routing contexts, with policy-controlled sharing. A virtual routing and forwarding instance, or VRF, is one such context. Gateway servers handle external traffic and address translation. Their required capacity depends on connection rates, throughput, and latency, so it need not grow in direct proportion to accelerator count. Address translation, or NAT, is not a complete substitute for the required security policy. The reference notes that fine-grained allow and deny rules can require supplemental firewall or access-control components. Review the permitted paths, return traffic, isolation, observability, and failure behavior together. Keep the contributed implementation distinct from the general responsibilities every selected design must satisfy.

slides.title: Select a Profile for Two Service Requirements
slides.transcript: Compare two services. The first serves a model entirely within one server for each request. Requests are independent and enter through a gateway. The second splits a model across hosts and exchanges intermediate results on the request path. Which inference profile would you start from for each? Minimal Inference can fit the first service, provided its other assumptions hold. Distributed Inference supplies the back-end needed by the second. Now add a second question: what must be measured before accepting either choice? For the first, include gateway behavior and request latency under load. For the second, include the cross-host path and its congestion and failure behavior as well. These are starting designs to qualify, not performance guarantees attached to a profile name.

slides.title: Connect Declared Intent to the Fabric
slides.transcript: Connect the intended design to the operating fabric. The April references use Hedgehog as a Kubernetes-native controller and SONiC on the switches. This is a contributed implementation example. The wiring definitions describe switches, servers, and connections. Separate tenant definitions describe network membership and permitted external connectivity. Kubernetes custom resource definitions, or CRDs, make that intent reviewable and versioned. The controller reconciles the intended state through agents on the switches. Observed state and telemetry then help operators check what is actually running. Preserve an independent out-of-band management path. The implementation deliberately avoids making that recovery network depend on the controller-managed network it may need to repair. Reusable logical intent still depends on supported hardware and verified platform behavior.

slides.title: Build Evidence through the Operating Lifecycle
slides.transcript: Carry one evidence packet through the operating lifecycle. At Day Zero, enroll the switches, establish identity, apply the supported platform profile, and verify basic reachability. Zero-touch provisioning automates part of that process; it does not remove the need to check its outcome. At Day One, compare the actual connections with the selected maps and apply the intended network and tenant policies. Record the validation results. At Day Two, observe the running service, detect drift, and manage changes and recovery. The animation keeps the same packet as those records accumulate. A change to hardware, wiring, policy, or software can require updating the relevant evidence. Controlled rollout, a recovery plan, and an identified owner make the handoff usable after initial installation.

slides.title: Choose Tests That Match the Claim
slides.transcript: Choose a test that can establish the claim. A document review can identify missing requirements. Schema and connectivity checks can establish logical consistency. A virtual lab can help teams practice configuration, reconciliation, and failure procedures. It does not establish physical cable behavior, full-scale throughput, or production latency. Those claims need representative equipment, workloads, load conditions, and failure tests. Separate what you measure from the target you accept. A service-level indicator, or SLI, is a measurement such as a latency percentile or error rate. A service-level objective, or SLO, is the target chosen for that measurement. The reference provides observability guidance; it does not prescribe one universal target. Similarly, enabling a switch's RDMA traffic policy does not validate the host-to-host result. Record the configuration, conditions, result, owner, and remaining limitation.

slides.title: Decide Whether the Proposal Is Ready
slides.transcript: Review this proposal. A service that previously ran within one host now shards its model across hosts. The equipment list and connection diagram disagree, and the only test report comes from a virtual lab. Is the proposal ready for deployment acceptance? First, identify the new cross-host dependency and select the required back-end configuration. Reconcile the equipment and endpoint records for that configuration. Confirm the physical installation and recovery paths. Then request representative workload, isolation, gateway, and failure evidence against the agreed targets. The appropriate decision is to keep the unmet acceptance items open, with owners and planned checks. This is the same method throughout the course: start with the changed requirement, follow the affected boundaries, and ask for evidence that can support the claim.

term_glossary.tooltip: A generic special-purpose accelerator. This course uses eight-xPU servers where the cited reference specifies that form factor.
Open Pod Group for M xPUs: a modular building block containing compute domains and their networking, storage, management and supporting resources.
xPU Open Cluster for N xPUs: a complete scale-out cluster containing one or more pod groups and the needed shared cluster resources.
The CPU-facing network. January calls it scale-out CPU; April uses SO-C/front-end terminology. Whether it is separate from storage depends on the selected configuration.
Management and service traffic using host-facing network paths. Its function and physical separation depend on the selected design.
A separate path to hardware management controllers, intended to remain usable for recovery when host or production-network functions are unavailable.
A list of equipment and quantities for a particular configuration. Reconcile it with layouts and connection records before procurement.
A port arrangement or cable that exposes multiple lower-rate connections from a higher-rate port. Each connection retains its own endpoint identity.
Scale-out NICs with the same accelerator-affinity index across servers. Rail-optimized attachment can preserve locality for matching-rail communication.
In single-homed Clos wiring, the servers attached to a common leaf. Permitted traffic between those servers can remain at that leaf.
A grouping of servers whose matching-rail NICs attach to a common leaf or specified leaf set. Cross-rail traffic may still need the spine.
Remote Direct Memory Access: direct data transfer between host memory regions using supported endpoints and transport. End-to-end configuration and testing remain necessary.
RDMA over Converged Ethernet, commonly pronounced rocky. The cited implementation applies traffic-class, congestion and flow-control settings for the designated RDMA traffic.
Virtual Routing and Forwarding: a separate routing context used here to implement tenant network boundaries. Permitted sharing requires explicit policy.
Network Address Translation: mapping addresses, and sometimes ports, between network contexts. It does not replace all required firewall or access-control policy.
Kubernetes Custom Resource Definition: an extension used by the contributed implementation to describe wiring or network intent in reviewable resources.
Software for Open Networking in the Cloud: the network operating system used on the switches in the contributed fabric implementation.
Automated enrollment and initial setup of supported devices. Operators still need to verify identity, reachability and the applied platform profile.
Service Level Indicator: a measured quantity such as latency, throughput or error rate. It describes observed behavior under stated conditions.
Service Level Objective: an operator-defined target for a measured indicator. A reference example is not a universal service target.
An environment for practicing configuration and operating workflows. The cited VLAB does not establish physical media behavior or production-scale performance.
